💡 Key Takeaways
  • Across the 17 deals reported on by FinTech Global this week, there was a total of $991m raised – showcasing a continuous strength in firms securing investment.
  • This was up on last week, where total of $602m was raised across 14 FinTech deals, a small increase on the previous week where $454.4m was raised across 12 deals.
  • Two of the top deals this week came from Bulgarian PayTech firm Payhawk and Model ML, a personal AI platform for financial and professional services.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Across the 17 deals reported on by FinTech Global this week, there was a total of $991m raised – showcasing a continuous strength in firms securing investment.

This was up on last week, where total of $602m was raised across 14 FinTech deals, a small increase on the previous week where $454.4m was raised across 12 deals.

Two of the top deals this week came from Bulgarian PayTech firm Payhawk and Model ML, a personal AI platform for financial and professional services.

Geographically, the US secured the most deals this week with 8 in total. Trailing in second was Canada with three, whilst Israel, Egypt, Spain, Georgia, the UK and Bulgaria pulled in one.

Market-wise, financial infrastructure firms made up the majority of this week’s deals with four. In joint second were WealthTech and CyberTech firms on three, PayTech, InsurTech and Blockchain firms secured two.

This week, research from FinTech Global showcased findings of a powerful performance for Global FinTech in this year’s third quarter. The Global FinTech market attracted $27.5bn across 1,275 deals in Q3 2026. Funding climbed 35% from $20.3bn in Q3 2025 but fell 11% from $30.9bn in Q2 2026.

Deal volume fell 2% from 1,306 transactions in Q3 2025 and rose 5% from 1,220 in Q2 2026.

Payhawk raises $280m to build AI-era Finance OS.

According to recent reports, payhawk, the Sofia-founded spend management and finance platform, has closed a $280m Series C round led by Growth Equity at Goldman Sachs Alternatives. The deal values the company at $2bn.

The raise takes Payhawk’s total funding past $515m. Every existing backer returned for the round, among them QED, Greenoaks, Lightspeed, Hedosophia and Bek Ventures.

They were joined by first-time investors Galdana Ventures, Cogito Capital, Inveready and Invus, as well as European founders Tomas Okmanas and Didac Lee.

Model ML bags $250m to give every banker an AI agent.

Model ML, a London-based personal AI platform for financial and professional services, has secured $250m in a Series B round that values the company at $1.5bn.

General Atlantic and QED Investors co-led the investment. Evolution Equity Partners, Airtree, Forestay Capital, Y Combinator, FT Partners, Latitude, Inception Fund and 13Books Capital also took part. The deal lifts the total capital raised by Model ML to $350m.

The raise comes after a period of rapid expansion. Over the third quarter of 2026, annual recurring revenue at the firm increased twelvefold compared with the same period a year earlier, while daily active users rose 26-fold.

Blue J lands $176m to put AI agents on tax desks.

Blue J, a tax research and advisory platform, has secured $176m in a Series E round that values the business at above $700m, as it moves beyond answering tax questions to handing the actual workload over to AI agents.

According to recent reports, JMI Equity, a growth equity investor, led the raise. Existing backers Oak HC/FT and Sapphire Ventures returned for the round, joined by Intrepid Growth Partners. The valuation also exceeds C$1bn. As part of the deal, JMI Equity principal Jack Duane will take a seat on the Blue J board.

The company intends to put the capital behind Workflows, its agentic AI product for tax practitioners, and to push further into the United Kingdom and other international markets.

Corma hits $1bn valuation with $125m Series A.

Corma, an AI research lab building foundation models for defensive cybersecurity, has secured $125m in Series A funding at a $1bn valuation, only three months after revealing its seed round.

NEA led the investment, with participation from returning backers Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures and Coatue. The latest raise takes the tech giant’s total funding to $185m.

Corma’s $60m seed round, led by Sequoia, was announced in August.

TBC Georgia secures $51m as ADB and IFC back trade finance.

TBC Georgia, a leading Georgian financial institution and member of the London-listed TBC Bank Group, has raised $51m from international commercial banks to widen the availability of trade finance for businesses across Georgia.

The capital comes with guarantee backing from the Asian Development Bank (ADB) and the International Finance Corporation (IFC).

Recent findings suggest that it is channelled through two established schemes: the ADB’s Trade and Supply Chain Finance Program and the IFC’s Global Trade Finance Program. Because both institutions stand behind the facility, commercial lenders can extend capital to the Georgian market with added assurance.

Codex lands $30m Series A to scale stablecoin FX.

Codex, a platform that provides foreign exchange infrastructure for stablecoins and fiat currencies, has secured $30m in Series A funding to expand its cross-border payments business.

Pantera headed the investment, which also drew backing from Dragonfly, Coinbase Ventures, Tenet, Reciprocal, Fin Capital, LeadBlock and additional investors. The deal puts the company’s post-money valuation at $130m.

Both Dragonfly and Coinbase Ventures have backed Codex before, having taken part in its seed round.

Arva AI lands $20m Series A for AI banking agents.

Arva AI, a manufacturer that deploys AI agents to make critical banking decisions, has secured $20m in Series A funding as it looks to push its accuracy-focused technology deeper into the bank back office.

Recent findings suggest that according to the company, most back-office decisions at banks are still made manually, but this has begun to shift. Over the past year, Arva’s customers started entrusting notable decisions to its agents, with staff setting policies and monitoring outcomes.

During that period the firm rolled out its technology at scale with banks and FinTechs, among them a top-10 US bank, a payments institution listed on the S&P 500 and the global FinTech Wise.

StepSecurity bags $20m as supply chain attacks escalate.

Elephant led the round, and existing backers Runtime Ventures, Inner Loop Capital and SaaS Ventures also took part. Together with a $3m seed round raised earlier, the deal lifts StepSecurity’s total funding to $23m.

The company plans to use the money to speed up development and wider rollout of its platform, which is designed to stop malicious packages at every checkpoint of the agentic software pipeline.

Vero Security raises $11m as AI security jobs go unstaffed.

Vero Security, a start-up developing a platform for AI Security Engineering, has closed an $11m seed round as large enterprises struggle to staff a responsibility that most still treat as a side duty.

According to recent reports, TLV Partners led the investment, joined by GTM Capital, Maple Capital and a group of angel backers. Vero was established in 2025 and has already signed several Fortune 500 businesses as customers.

Alongside the raise, it is introducing AISecurityEngineering.org, an open community and knowledge hub offering practical field guides, workshops and the ASE credential track for practitioners shaping this upcoming specialism.

Roadzen raises $10m for India arm at $300m valuation.

Roadzen, which applies AI to insurance and mobility, has secured roughly $10m (₹94 crore) for its Indian subsidiary, Roadzen AI Limited, which is now valued at about $300m post-money on a stand-alone basis.

The round is being raised entirely as common equity. It carries no warrants or preferred rights, and the new shares rank equally with those held by the existing shareholder, Roadzen.

Sources indicate that because the capital goes into the subsidiary, shareholders in the Nasdaq-listed parent will not be diluted. Family offices and capital markets investors anchored the deal. Several of them had backed the company’s earlier India subsidiary round and raised their commitments this time.

Valeria bags €5.5m seed to scale AI payroll engine.

Valeria, a Barcelona-headquartered payroll and workforce management platform built on artificial intelligence, has secured €5.5m in seed funding to expand its technology for businesses that see frequent staff changes.

Industry observers note that the round was led by BlackFin, with returning backers VentureFriends and Fortino also participating. GoHub Ventures came on board as a latest investor in the company.

The seed raise follows a €1.7m pre-seed round completed in February 2026, meaning Valeria has secured over €7m in total during 2026.

WealthTech finny raises Rs 5.3 Cr angel round.

finny, a WealthTech start-up offering personalised financial advice, has reportedly secured Rs 5.3 Cr (around $560,000) through an angel round, according to a report from BW Disrupt.

A group of high-profile backers joined the round. Among them were Ramanathan RV, who founded both Hyperface and Juspay, and Anil Goel, who serves as Global CTO at Nielsen. Uday Sodhi, previously an executive at Sony Pictures, also took part, as did Aditya Pittie, MD and CEO of Pittie Group. Angel syndicate Zorvian LLP was among the other participants.

According to recent reports, the company intends to split the newly introduced money across three priorities. A portion will go towards R&D, with an emphasis on building out its AI-driven products.

Pretxt raises $5m to keep AI agents within the rules.

Pretxt, a newly rolled out enterprise AI manufacturer focused on runtime oversight of AI agents, has stepped out of stealth mode with $5m in seed capital to build out a technology category it calls AI Supervision.

Recent findings suggest that deciens Capital, Howdy Partners, Service Provider Capital and NSV Wolf Capital backed the round. Pretxt looks to use the capital to bring its supervision layer to enterprises that want AI agents to handle higher-stakes work without drifting from approved procedures.

Sources indicate that AI agents no longer simply produce text. They now speak with customers, connect to other systems, handle transactions and run business processes. According to Pretxt, these agents do not always behave as instructed.

Verlo raises $4.5m to cut admin work for wealth firms.

Verlo, a provider of an AI operating system built for wealth management firms, has secured $4.5m CAD in seed funding to help Registered Investment Advisors (RIAs) cut back on time-consuming administrative tasks.

Sources indicate that staircase Ventures led the investment, while Pelorus VC came back to back the manufacturer again. They were joined by several angel investors, among them founders and senior executives from Verafin, the Newfoundland financial crime software business that Nasdaq bought in 2020 for $2.7bn.

Global Kiwi Labs raises $4m for TheHUB.

Global Kiwi Labs, the developer behind digital asset colocation network TheHUB, has closed a $4m seed round as it looks to bring the equal-access trading architecture used by major traditional exchanges to digital asset markets.

Valor Capital Group led the round. Adderall Capital, Keyrock and Staking Facilities also invested, alongside a small number of angel backers.

According to recent reports, theHUB’s first site, which is located within the Equinix TY15 data centre in Tokyo and is now live and bringing on exchanges, trading firms and validators. The company will also use the money to add engineers to its team and move into further regions.

Connect Money raises $3.5m to enter Saudi Arabia and Morocco.

According to recent reports, AWS Lambda now supports creating serverless applications using Python 3.15. Python 3.15 is generally available for Lambda Event Functions and is available in public preview for Lambda Web Functions. This is the first Python runtime for Web Functions, which until now only supported Node.js. With this launch, developers can also build web applications and APIs on Web Functions in Python. Developers can use Python 3.15 as both a managed runtime and a base container image (Event Functions only), and AWS will automatically apply updates to the managed runtime and base image as they become available. Python 3.15 is the latest release of Python. With this release, you can use the latest Python 3.15 features in Lambda, such as explicit lazy imports that can reduce function startup time, the new frozendict and sentinel built-in types, and an improved JIT compiler. You can use Python 3.15 with Powertools for AWS Lambda (Python), a developer toolkit to implement serverless best practices and increase developer velocity. You can also use the full range of AWS deployment tools, including the Lambda console, AWS CLI, AWS Serverless Application Model (AWS SAM), AWS CDK, and AWS CloudFormation to deploy and manage serverless applications written in Python 3.15. The Python 3.15 runtime is available in all Regions where Event Functions and Web Functions are available. For more information about Python 3.15 in Lambda, refer to the Event Function and Web Function documentation. For more information about AWS Lambda, visit our product page.

#20326. Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

📅 29 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1297 w)

Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1297 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.
  • Recent findings suggest that today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research.
  • The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

Recent findings suggest that today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

Participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Recent findings suggest that the U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to proposal for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

But making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

According to recent reports, project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

The demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

The pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many upcoming science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

Sources indicate that figure 1. Fresh public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

In a recent development, when organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an important part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

Publicly available genomic data has proved crucial in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support latest research that others can build upon.

Sources indicate that this is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

It has been revealed that making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an important first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

To explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:.

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026.

Recent findings suggest that the inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

Participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

It has been revealed that beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

Teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge.

The CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be revealed through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or manufacturer building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

We also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding upcoming expertise on a single endpoint.

It has been revealed that granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this upgrade. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the newly introduced multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.

#20322. Transformers Model Integration Contracts

Transformers Model Integration Contracts

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1284 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5.
  • According to recent reports, when we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them.
  • Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is massive: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

According to recent reports, when we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is massive: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

According to recent reports, our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

Sources indicate that transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:.

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

According to recent reports, A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:.

It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

Recent findings suggest that one detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

Recent findings suggest that we then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

Industry observers note that we also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

The Llama 4 Scout shrink report reveals what this looks like on a substantial model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

Sources indicate that our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a fresh model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:.

Industry observers note that it drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

Industry observers note that we used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

Industry observers note that with random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:.

The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

Sources indicate that so we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:.

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

t5/umt5 in a blog post in 2026, never thought I’d see the day 😍.

CWE-bench v2: More coverage, quality, and transparency

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (591 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities.
  • It has been revealed that our goal is to be exhaustive.
  • As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI, CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set, so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai.

It has been revealed that our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:.

Every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.

Results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file (how). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the CWE-bench leaderboard Space, where latest models are added through a PR on the Space.

Open-weight models, from the dataset page:.

All evaluated models, including API-only ones:.

Of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.

On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

Sources indicate that every task is a self-contained Harbor task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json. Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself:.

Sources indicate that -k 4 runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the dataset page first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once:.

The tasks are also tagged rl-environment: the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.

Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus is a fully managed, Prometheus-compatible monitoring service, that helps you monitor and alert on operational metrics at scale. Customers in the AWS European Sovereign Cloud can now run Prometheus-compatible monitoring workloads in-region, which lowers latency for local workloads and keeps metric data within the region.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, you can now upgrade existing Amazon MSK Provisioned clusters from Standard brokers to Express brokers in place, with fully managed data migration and no application changes.
  • Express brokers make Apache Kafka simpler to manage and more cost-effective to run at scale, with pay-as-you-go storage that scales automatically and built-in best practice defaults for higher resilience.
  • In a recent development, in-place upgrade is available for MSK Provisioned clusters running Standard brokers on Apache Kafka version 3.9 with KRaft, in all AWS Regions where Express brokers are available.

In a recent development, you can now upgrade existing Amazon MSK Provisioned clusters from Standard brokers to Express brokers in place, with fully managed data migration and no application changes. Express brokers are designed to deliver up to 3x more throughput per broker, scale up to 20x faster, and recover up to 90% faster compared to Standard brokers. With in-place upgrade, you can get the performance and operational benefits of Express brokers in hours, without needing to create a fresh cluster or having to migrate your data and applications to it. The upgrade keeps cluster endpoints unchanged, eliminating application cutovers, and preserves consumer offsets, so stateful applications such as Apache Flink and Kafka Streams continue without reprocessing or duplicates.

Express brokers make Apache Kafka simpler to manage and more cost-effective to run at scale, with pay-as-you-go storage that scales automatically and built-in best practice defaults for higher resilience. Previously, upgrading to Express brokers meant creating a upcoming cluster and migrating workloads to it, which required careful planning and cross-team coordination. With this launch, you can upgrade your existing Standard brokers to Express brokers in-place, without interrupting your applications, while maintaining complete control over the upgrade process. The upgrade adds Express brokers to your cluster and moves your topics to them, either automatically or in batches you control. Your Standard brokers stay in the cluster until you choose to decommission them to complete the upgrade, so you can validate your applications and roll back if needed.

In a recent development, in-place upgrade is available for MSK Provisioned clusters running Standard brokers on Apache Kafka version 3.9 with KRaft, in all AWS Regions where Express brokers are available. You can upgrade to Express brokers on M7g or M8g instances. Express brokers on M8g deliver up to 30% cost savings compared to Express brokers on M7g. There's no additional charge for the upgrade itself. You pay for both Standard and Express brokers while the upgrade is in progress. To get started, visit the Amazon MSK Developer Guide and the Migration to Express brokers product page.

#20318. Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1703 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1703 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one.
  • Sources indicate that both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language.
  • Sources indicate that palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all.

Sources indicate that both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other.

Sources indicate that palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language, and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it.

A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at.

It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from.

It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide indicates and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent.

There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them.

Sources indicate that nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one notes, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter:.

Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster.

We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×.

According to recent reports, there's no public corpus of prepares, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides.

It has been revealed that every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example:.

"Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance.".

The coder reasons about geometry:.

In a recent development, "The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart.".

The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example.

The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest.

What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions.

Users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives, short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]]:.

The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead.

The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase.

Figure 1. An illustration of the same initiative without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive.

Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first.

Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned.

First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code.

The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse.

Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right).

Recent findings suggest that to measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average.

Sources indicate that we evaluate on PresentBench, which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a strategy, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper.

According to recent reports, figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean.

Sources indicate that palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model.

PresentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close.

In a recent development, the harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training.

We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining.

Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts:.

Recent findings suggest that AWS is announcing the general availability of new low-cost burstable Amazon EC2 T9g instances, which offer the best price performance among general-purpose EC2 instances. These instances are powered by AWS Graviton5 processors and built on the latest sixth generation AWS Nitro cards. T9g instances deliver up to 45% better price performance compared to previous generation T4g instances, and offer four sizes: nano, micro, small, and medium. These instances are designed for workloads requiring low to moderate CPU utilization, including data processing, login gateways, small databases, microservices, low-traffic websites, freemium services, staging and development, and short-duration compute tasks such as batch processing, event-driven functions, and CI/CD pipelines.

T9g instances deliver up to 2.3x the compute performance, 1.5x higher network bandwidth, and 2.8x higher EBS bandwidth compared to T4g instances. They are built on the sixth-generation AWS Nitro System and feature the Nitro Isolation Engine, harnessing formal verification to provide mathematical assurance that customer workloads are isolated from each other and AWS operators, pioneering a fresh standard for mathematically proven cloud security.

T9g instances use the same CPU credit system as T4g with Standard and Unlimited modes, so existing T customers can upgrade to T9g and immediately benefit from better price performance, enabling them to lower their TCO. For customers upcoming to AWS or migrating from on-premises, T9g instances provide one of the most cost-effective entry points to run a variety of lightweight workloads.

T9g.micro and T9g.small are available under the AWS Free Tier. T9g instances are available in US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (N. California, Oregon), Canada (Central), South America (São Paulo), Europe (Frankfurt, Spain), and Asia Pacific (Malaysia, Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo) regions. T9g instances are available to purchase via Savings Plans, On-Demand instances, and Spot instances. To learn more, visit the Amazon EC2 T9g instances page.

#20316. Latest Update: Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1273 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1273 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.
  • In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms.
  • Industry observers note that OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.

In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.

Industry observers note that OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.

However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.

Run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.

A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.

Recent findings suggest that so we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.

According to recent reports, say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:.

According to recent reports, the choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.

Either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.

The base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a newly introduced 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.

The data is organized into three streams:.

All three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.

In a recent development, the full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.

We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.

Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).

Cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.

This is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.

According to recent reports, SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.

On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.

On a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.

A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.

This isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.

Parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem.

Recent findings suggest that try it on your own documents here. To learn more about Dharma-AI and the specialized models we build, visit dharma-ai.com.

Explore Dharma AI on Hugging Face to try our interactive demos, download our open-source models, and discover how specialized AI systems outperform general-purpose models in real enterprise applications.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device.
  • We've been very happy with the reception so far.
  • According to recent reports, most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.

We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.

According to recent reports, most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate.

Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.

According to recent reports, we revealed Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.

In a recent development, phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.

In a recent development, phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio. Phonon also handles the notable things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.

It has been revealed that it runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now. Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.

Sources indicate that the launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.

The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.

In a recent development, developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.

Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.

The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very newly introduced project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub, the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.

On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish, and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.

Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.

We built a upcoming inference framework, ptts, specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).

Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.

Recent findings suggest that it belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.

Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer, held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:.

It has been revealed that A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices.

The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:.

generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:.

Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in Gradium Studio. Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.

We also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.

Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.

Sources indicate that phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build.

According to recent reports, congrats on the launch — running this cleanly on an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off is genuinely impressive. As a German speaker I'm happy to see it top the intelligibility ranking in German; the compounding is unforgiving to TTS, so that's not a small win.

One line in "what's next" I keep coming back to: Korean, Arabic and Japanese get offered as custom-training requests. That framing quietly shows where the field's centre of gravity still sits — a handful of languages are first-class citizens, and everything else is a sales conversation. The Open TTS Leaderboard covering 23 languages is a great step, but the long tail of the world's languages is still waiting. Would love to see lower-resource languages get first-class leaderboard slots rather than a custom quote.
